title: Rolle's Theorem
quickIdea: If f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable inside, and f(a) = f(b), then f' is zero somewhere strictly between a and b.
remember: Three hypotheses: f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b]; f is differentiable on the open interval (a, b); f(a) = f(b).
Conclusion: there is at least one c with a < c < b and f'(c) = 0. The point is strictly inside, never at an endpoint.
Geometrically: somewhere between the two equal heights the tangent is horizontal.

Why it is true: the extreme value theorem gives a maximum and a minimum on [a, b]. If either is attained inside, Fermat's theorem makes f' zero there. If both are at the ends, then f equals f(a) everywhere and f' is zero throughout.
Every hypothesis is load-bearing: |x| on [-1, 1] is continuous with equal endpoint values, but it is not differentiable at 0 and no interior point has zero slope.

example.prompt: Verify Rolle's theorem for f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3 on [1, 3] and find every c it guarantees.
example.work: A polynomial is continuous and differentiable everywhere, and f(1) = 1 - 4 + 3 = 0 while f(3) = 9 - 12 + 3 = 0, so all three hypotheses hold. f'(x) = 2x - 4 vanishes only at x = 2, and 2 lies in (1, 3).
example.answer: c = 2. It is the only such point, and f(2) = -1 is the lowest value on the interval.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2014 Set 1 Q.6 is the pure Rolle question in disguise: the function is a 3x3 determinant, and the equal endpoint values come from two rows becoming identical. The exam pattern is always the same - establish the three hypotheses from the structure of the function, then quote the theorem instead of differentiating.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2014 Set 1 Q.6: f(theta) is the determinant with rows (sin, cos, tan) at theta, at pi/6 and at pi/3, on [pi/6, pi/3]. Are these true? I: some theta in the open interval has f'(theta) = 0. II: some theta in the open interval has f'(theta) != 0.
variations.why: I is Rolle, because f(pi/6) = 0 and f(pi/3) = 0 by two identical rows. II needs the extra observation that f is not constant, which the value f(pi/4) = 0.0977 settles.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Apply Rolle's theorem to f(x) = x^3 - 4x on [-2, 2] and list every guaranteed point.
variations.answer: c = 2/sqrt(3) and c = -2/sqrt(3), both about 1.155 in absolute value.
variations.why: f(-2) = 0 = f(2) and f'(x) = 3x^2 - 4, so the candidates are the two roots of 3c^2 = 4. The variation tests the 'at least one' wording: the theorem is satisfied twice over.

trap.what: Quoting Rolle whenever the function is continuous and differentiable, without checking f(a) = f(b).
trap.why: The equal endpoint values are a hypothesis, not a formality. Drop it and the conclusion can be false.
trap.counterexample: f(x) = x^2 on [0, 2] is continuous and differentiable, but f(0) = 0 and f(2) = 4, and f'(x) = 2x is never zero in (0, 2). The right tool there is the mean value theorem, which gives c = 1 with f'(1) = 2 equal to the average slope 4/2.

check.question: Does Rolle's theorem apply to f(x) = x^(2/3) on [-1, 1], and does its conclusion hold?
check.answer: It does not apply, and the conclusion is false.
check.explanation: f(-1) = 1 = f(1) and f is continuous, but f'(x) = (2/3) x^(-1/3) does not exist at 0, so the differentiability hypothesis fails. For x != 0 the derivative is never zero, so no interior point has zero slope - exactly the failure the missing hypothesis allows.
